exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with pallor and splenomegaly; smear shows 30 % elliptocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis and next diagnostic step? — Identify hereditary elliptocytosis; order CBC, retic count, and consider family history.
During a malaria outbreak, a child with known HE develops sudden Hb 5 g/dL. What immediate management is required? — Give urgent transfusion, treat malaria, and start folate.
How does hereditary pyropoikilocytosis differ from classic HE on smear? — HPP shows marked poikilocytosis after heat exposure and severe anemia in infancy.
A patient with chronic hemolysis develops right‑upper‑quadrant pain. What complication should you suspect and how to confirm? — Suspect pigmented gallstones; confirm with abdominal ultrasound.
Why is splenectomy contraindicated in a child with active malaria infection? — Removing the spleen impairs clearance of parasitized red cells, worsening malaria.
What laboratory test can be falsely normal in mild HE and how to proceed? — Osmotic fragility may be normal; rely on smear and clinical picture.
Explain why folate, not iron, is the key supplement in HE. — Hemolysis increases folate demand for erythropoiesis; iron stores are usually adequate.
A newborn of a mother with HE shows jaundice at 12 h. What urgent assessment is needed? — Check total bilirubin; if >15 mg/dL, start phototherapy to prevent kernicterus.
ai.title: Hereditary Elliptocytosis and Related Disorders
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Hereditary elliptocytosis (HE) and hereditary pyropoikilocytosis (HPP) are red‑cell membrane disorders causing elliptocytes on smear. They range from asymptomatic to severe hemolytic anemia, especially in low‑resource settings where infections can precipitate crises.

b: Elliptocytes: elongated cells with parallel sides, often >30 µm long
HPP: marked poikilocytosis after heat exposure, severe anemia in infancy
sections.p: HE and HPP are inherited defects of spectrin or protein 4.1R causing fragile, elongated red cells. Diagnosis rests on peripheral smear showing >25 % elliptocytes and family history.

b: Mild: Hb > 10 g/dL, no transfusion
Moderate: Hb 8‑10 g/dL, occasional transfusion
Severe: Hb < 8 g/dL, regular transfusion or splenectomy
sections.p: Severity is graded by hemoglobin level, transfusion need, and presence of complications.

b: Spectrin gene mutation – most common
Protein 4.1R mutation – often HPP phenotype
Co‑existing malaria or severe infection – precipitates crisis
sections.p: Most cases are autosomal dominant mutations in spectrin (SPTA1, SPTB) or protein 4.1R (EPB41). In East Africa, co‑existing malaria, sickle‑cell trait, or HIV can worsen hemolysis.

b: Chronic mild anemia, splenomegaly
Acute drop in Hb after infection or fever (HPP)
Pigmented gallstones in long‑standing hemolysis
sections.p: Children may be asymptomatic or present with pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly, and gallstones. HPP presents in infancy with severe anemia after fever or heat exposure.
Investigations focus on confirming the red‑cell defect and assessing severity.

t.b: What cell morphology looks like – presence of >25 % elliptocytes confirms diagnosis
How severe the anemia is – Hb level guides severity staging
What marrow response is – elevated retics indicate hemolysis
What type of jaundice – indirect rise supports hemolysis
What membrane stability is – increased fragility supports hereditary elliptocytosis
What mutation is present – confirms diagnosis; if unavailable, rely on smear and family history

b: Acute hemolytic crisis with Hb < 6 g/dL
Severe hyperbilirubinemia causing kernicterus in newborns
Gallstone disease leading to biliary colic or cholangitis
Splenic sequestration in children with massive splenomegaly
sections.p: Complications arise from severe hemolysis and its sequelae.

b: Folate supplementation – supports erythropoiesis
Avoid heat exposure and high fevers – reduces HPP crises
Prompt treatment of malaria, bacterial infections, or HIV – removes precipitating factors
Transfusion for severe anemia – only when Hb < 6 g/dL or symptomatic
Splenectomy in refractory severe cases – reduces hemolysis but increases infection risk
sections.p: Treat the hemolysis, prevent triggers, and address complications.

b: CBC every 3‑6 months in moderate disease
Ultrasound for gallstones after 5 years of hemolysis
Vaccination against encapsulated organisms before splenectomy
Genetic counseling for families
sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents complications and guides timing of interventions.

Genetic testing may miss rare variants; rely on morphology and family history
